chunks: "The question is cut off, so I'll assume you mean far from the amplifier or the ADC.

The problem is that the raw sense voltage is only tens of millivolts, at a fairly high impedance, and I'd be sending it across the board, past switch nodes, picking up noise in proportion to the length and loop area.
Noise is injected onto the line whatever the signal is, so the best fix is to make the signal big before it travels. So I'd move the amplifier to the resistor.
Put the current-sense amp right at the Kelvin pickoff, so the long run carries a few-volt, low-impedance signal, or a digital value if I use a power-monitor chip with I2C or SPI at the resistor.
With a gain of 50, the signal-to-noise ratio on the long run improves by 50, which is 34 decibels.

If I can't move the amplifier, I'd keep the raw pair tight and matched, over a continuous plane, with ground vias beside it, or use a twisted pair or shielded cable off board, filtered at the receiving end.
And I'd route the amplifier's reference back to the resistor's ground side, so the load current in the ground plane doesn't add an offset.
If the grounds really differ, an isolated amplifier."
